title: Surface Tension: Water's Stretchy Skin
hook: Water acts like it's wrapped in an invisible elastic skin — strong enough to let a bug walk across a pond and pull a droplet into a near-perfect sphere.
key_points: Liquid molecules attract each other; those at the surface get pulled inward and sideways.
This makes the surface contract to the smallest area, like a stretched membrane.
It lets water striders walk on ponds and a dense paperclip rest on water.
Soap weakens surface tension, helping water spread out and wet surfaces to clean them.
content_html: Look closely at a slightly overfilled glass and you'll see the water bulge above the rim without spilling, held by what looks like a thin skin. That skin is surface tension. Inside a liquid, every molecule is tugged equally in all directions by its neighbors. But a molecule at the surface has no neighbors above it, so the net pull is inward and sideways — which makes the surface behave like a stretched elastic membrane that tries to shrink to the smallest possible area.
extra_html: This is why a free-falling droplet pulls itself into a sphere, the shape with the least surface for its volume. It's also why a water strider can stride across a pond and why a carefully placed paperclip — denser than water — can rest on the surface without sinking: their weight simply isn't enough to break through. Surface tension even helps water climb narrow tubes against gravity, a key to how plants draw water upward. Soap and detergents work partly by lowering surface tension, letting water spread out, soak into fabric, and surround grease instead of beading up and rolling away. Wikipedia covers the molecular cause and its many everyday effects.

related.title: What Is Pressure?
related.hook: Pressure is force spread over an area. Concentrate the same push on a tiny spot and it skyrockets — which is why a sharp knife cuts and a thumbtack pierces.

related.title: States of Matter
related.hook: Solid, liquid, gas, plasma — the difference is how tightly particles are bound. Add heat and matter changes state, but during the change the temperature holds still.

related.title: Buoyancy: Why Things Float
related.hook: Any fluid pushes up on what's in it with a force equal to the weight of fluid it shoves aside. Match your weight that way and you float — that's Archimedes.

flashcards.prompt: What causes surface tension in a liquid?
flashcards.back_html: Molecules attract their neighbors. Those at the surface have no neighbors above, so they're pulled inward and sideways, making the surface contract.

flashcards.prompt: How can a water strider walk on a pond without sinking?

choices.text: Surface tension forms a skin-like surface that supports its light weight
It is lighter than air and floats above the water
Its legs are magnetically repelled by water

flashcards.explanation_html: Its weight isn't enough to break through the contracted surface, so the water's tension holds it up — no need to be less dense than water.

flashcards.prompt: Why does adding soap help water clean greasy dishes?

choices.text: Soap lowers surface tension, letting water spread and wet surfaces better
Soap raises surface tension so water beads up and rolls off
Soap makes water denser so it sinks into grease

flashcards.explanation_html: Plain water beads up because of high surface tension; soap reduces it so water can spread into crevices and lift away grease.
